title: Stanford's Tutor CoPilot (GPT-4 guidance for human tutors) raises K-12 math mastery 4 percentage points in a 900-tutor randomized trial with FEV Tutor
summary: RCT with 900 tutors and 1,800 grade 3–8 students in a southern US district: students whose tutors had Tutor CoPilot were 4 points more likely to master topics; 9 points for lower-rated tutors.
account: Wang, Ribeiro, Robinson, Loeb and Demszky of Stanford built Tutor CoPilot, a language-model system that gives human tutors expert-like suggestions during live sessions. They tested it with FEV Tutor, a virtual tutoring provider, and a large southern U.S. school district serving over 30,000 students. Nine schools took part. The district identified 1,787 students in grades 3–8, 80% Hispanic, who had performed below grade level. The preprint (arXiv, 3 October 2024) says the study started at the end of March 2024 and lasted two months. The 900 tutors were evenly split between treatment and control. Students of treated tutors were 4 percentage points more likely to master topics. Students of lower-rated tutors gained 9 points, at about $20 per tutor per year. Education Week (31 October 2024), quoting co-author Susanna Loeb, reported that tutors using the tool were more likely to prompt students to explain. They were less likely to give away solutions. The 74 (7 October 2024) and MIT Technology Review (28 October 2024) reported that the system runs on OpenAI's GPT-4. They gave pass rates of 66% versus 62% on exit assessments and quoted outside researchers' caveats about the basic level of the mathematics. The date observed is the first day of the month in which the trial began, used as a placeholder. The preprint says the study started at the end of March 2024.
purpose: Tutor CoPilot was built to scale expert tutoring guidance to novice tutors in real time. Higher student mastery is that purpose.
system: Tutor CoPilot: language-model assistant giving real-time pedagogical suggestions to human tutors on FEV Tutor's platform
model_version: GPT-4 (per The 74 and MIT Technology Review)
developer: Stanford University researchers (Wang, Ribeiro, Robinson, Loeb, Demszky)
deployer: FEV Tutor with a large southern U.S. school district (nine schools)

ratings.reason: General benefit without an individually attributable event. Students of tutors with the tool were 4 percentage points more likely to master topics, 9 points for lower-rated tutors (preprint abstract).
General benefit without an event: the tutoring provider's lower-rated tutors improved most at about $20 per tutor annually (preprint abstract).

ai_role.statement: The model advised the human tutor and never taught the student directly. The measured change runs through tutor behavior (more prompting for explanations, fewer given-away solutions). Outside researchers quoted by MIT Technology Review note the mathematics was relatively basic.

produced_by: A language model prompted with a taxonomy of expert tutoring moves rather than answers
Integration into a live virtual-tutoring platform where tutors can request suggestions mid-session
Tutor-level randomization (900 tutors) with preregistered analysis
must_hold: Human tutors willing to use suggestions in real time
Students below grade level in under-served schools, the population studied

headline: Stanford's Tutor CoPilot lifts math mastery 4 percentage points
metric: students of treated tutors were 4 percentage points more likely to master topics

comparator.against: students of control-group tutors on the same platform who did not have access to Tutor CoPilot
comparator.before: 62% student passing rate on exit tickets (control tutors)
comparator.after: 66% passing rate (tutors with Tutor CoPilot), 4 percentage points higher
comparator.quote: Students working with treatment tutors were 4 percentage points (p.p.) more likely to pass their exit tickets (p< 0.01, 62% → 66% student passing rate from control to treatment).

later.note: The preprint was revised again on 10 October 2026, but no later deployment, replication or publication of the trial was found.
